title: Manna (Exodus 16:1–21)
hook: bread from heaven each morning, enough for the day, and it rots if hoarded

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miriam's tambourine: a drum carried out of Egypt, and a call to sing to the Lord.

A month after the sea, the singing has stopped. They're in the wilderness of Sin, a stretch of desert, and the food from Egypt has run out. The people complain to Moses and Aaron, in the King James Bible: we wish we'd died in Egypt, "when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full." Flesh pots. Pots of meat. Slavery has become, in their memory, a buffet. Anyone who has missed a bad job because at least you knew what you were getting knows this feeling. And God's answer is not a lecture. It's breakfast.
screen: `A MONTH AFTER THE SEA.` → `THE FOOD RUNS OUT.` → `THE FLESH POTS OF EGYPT.`

segments.voice: "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you." In the morning, when the dew lifts, the ground is covered with something small and flaky, fine as frost. The people ask each other, in Hebrew, man hu? What is it? "It is manna: for they wist not what it was." They named their daily bread what is it. Exodus later says it tasted like wafers made with honey. Then the rules. Gather what each person needs for one day. Some gather more, some less, but when they measure it, "he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack." Everyone has enough. And don't keep any till morning. Some do anyway, just in case. By morning, "it bred worms, and stank." You can't stockpile this bread. You have to trust there'll be more tomorrow. Christians hear this story in the Lord's Prayer: "Give us this day our daily bread." Not this year's. Today's. Paul quotes the line about much and little when he asks one church to share with another, so that everyone has enough. And in John's Gospel, after feeding a crowd, Jesus talks about the manna and says: "I am the bread of life." Many Christians understand communion in that light. Not long ago, Joseph stored grain for seven years, and that was wise. Here is the other half of wisdom: some things can only be received one day at a time.
screen: `MAN HU? WHAT IS IT?` · `MUCH HAD NOTHING OVER.` · `KEPT TILL MORNING, IT STANK.` · `GIVE US THIS DAY.` · then, large: `ENOUGH FOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: Think through today, the food, the shopping, the scrolling, and find one place where you gather more than today needs, just in case. Picture taking only enough, and notice the small fear that comes with it, then notice it pass. If you pray, you can pray the old words, give us this day our daily bread; if you don't, simply rest in enough.
Manna. From the Hebrew question man hu, what is it? The bread from heaven that came each morning in the wilderness, enough for one day.
Your line: enough for today. Tomorrow has its own morning, and its own bread. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians pray "give us this day our daily bread" in the Lord's Prayer, and many read John 6, where Jesus calls himself the bread of life, alongside the manna story, especially when teaching about communion.

trapdoor: what you thought: manna is a miracle food from heaven.
what it means: bread you can't hoard, given one day at a time, so that everyone has enough and no one has too much.
what a scholar hears: Exodus explains the name with man hu, what is it?; travelers have long compared manna to sweet resin found in Sinai, while the text treats it as God's daily gift.

chat.says: Why couldn't the Israelites save extra manna for later?
options: Kept till morning, it bred worms and stank; it came daily, enough for each day.
Moses rationed it strictly, so there was never any extra left to save.
Saving was allowed, but most people were too tired to carry any extra.
chat.meaning: The rule was enough for one day. Hoarded manna bred worms and stank, so they had to trust there'd be more tomorrow.

wilderness of Sin.meaning: the stretch of desert where the manna fell

notes: The KJV of 16:15 ('It is manna') reflects a reading of man hu as a statement; most modern readers take it as the question 'what is it?'. Confirm the script's handling.
Taste 'like wafers made with honey' from 16:31. Confirm.
The double portion on the sixth day for the Sabbath (16:22–30) falls just outside today's reading and is not mentioned.
